title: Leading with Questions: How Leaders Find the Right Solutions by Knowing What to Ask
author: Michael J. Marquardt
summary:
Michael Marquardt's central claim is disarmingly simple: the leaders who get the best results are not the ones with the best answers, but the ones who ask the best questions. Drawing on decades of research into "action learning" and on interviews with dozens of executives across industries and countries, Marquardt argues that most leaders are trained — by business school, by corporate culture, and by their own egos — to default to giving answers, directives, and solutions. That instinct feels efficient in the moment, but it quietly starves an organization of the very thing it needs to adapt: the honest information, creative ideas, and ownership that only surface when people are asked rather than told.

The book opens by making the negative case first. Marquardt walks through well-known organizational disasters — the sinking of the Titanic, the Challenger explosion, the Bay of Pigs invasion, and corporate collapses like Enron and WorldCom — and argues that each was preceded by a culture where dissenting questions were discouraged or simply never asked. Leaders and the people around them talked themselves past warning signs because no one felt safe, or curious enough, to ask "are we sure about this?" This sets up the book's larger argument: a "questioning culture" isn't a soft communication tactic, it's a risk-management and innovation system.

From there the book becomes practical. Marquardt distinguishes between the "Judger" mindset, which enters a conversation looking to evaluate, blame, or defend, and the "Learner" mindset, which enters genuinely curious about what's true and what's possible. He treats this mindset shift as the real skill underneath every specific questioning technique — asking a good question from a Judger stance still lands as an interrogation. Around this core he builds out craft: how to frame open versus closed questions, how to use silence and pacing, how to listen actively enough that people feel heard rather than processed, and how to follow up in a way that deepens rather than derails a conversation.

The final section of the book moves from individual skill to organizational system, showing how leaders in real companies — DuPont, Alcoa, Novartis, Cargill, and others — built questioning into supervision, coaching, team-building, and problem-solving. Marquardt is explicit that this is not about leaders abdicating direction-setting; it's about leaders getting better information before they set direction, and building teams that can think for themselves when the leader isn't in the room.

Where the book is most useful is in its refusal to treat "ask more questions" as a platitude. It gives leaders a diagnostic (Judger vs. Learner), a menu of techniques, and enough real-company case material to see what a questioning culture looks like in practice, rather than just why it's theoretically desirable. Its weakness, which several readers and reviewers note, is that the case for questions is made at some length before the book gets to the how — a reader in a hurry can skip most of Part One and lose little.

sections.title: The Power of Questions (Part I: A Powerful But Underused Leadership Tool / Benefits of a Questioning Culture)
sections.summary:
This opening part sets out to establish why questions matter more than most leaders assume, and why the default toward answering is actually a liability rather than a strength. Marquardt starts from the observation that most leaders are promoted and rewarded for having answers, which trains an entire class of executives to treat "I don't know" or "what do you think?" as a sign of weakness.

The substance of the section is a tour through documented organizational failures — the Titanic's crew ignoring iceberg warnings, NASA engineers not being asked (or not pushing) hard enough about the Challenger's O-rings, intelligence failures before the Bay of Pigs — used to show that catastrophic decisions are rarely the result of a single bad call, but of an environment where the right question never got asked out loud. Marquardt then flips to the upside case: organizations that deliberately built "questioning cultures" report better team engagement, faster problem surfacing, more innovation, and stronger cross-level trust, because people who are asked feel ownership that people who are told do not.

The section hands off to Part II by establishing that if questions are this valuable, the obvious next problem is that most people — leaders especially — are actually bad at asking them, which is where the book turns next.
keyLessons: A pattern of leaders answering instead of asking is a leading indicator of organizational risk, not just a communication style.
Psychological safety to raise a question is a prerequisite for catching problems before they become disasters.
A questioning culture increases engagement because it shifts people from being told what to do to co-owning the answer.

sections.title: Asking Questions Effectively (Part II: Why We Have Trouble with Questions / Asking the Right Questions / The Art of Asking Questions / Creating a Questioning Culture)
sections.summary:
This part sets out to move from "why questions matter" to "how to actually ask them well," and it is the technical core of the book. It opens by diagnosing why even willing leaders struggle: fear of looking incompetent, impatience, a habit of asking questions that are really statements in disguise ("don't you think we should...?"), and simple lack of practice.

The middle of the section introduces the book's signature framework, the Judger/Learner mindset distinction, arguing that the same words land completely differently depending on whether the asker is trying to evaluate and fix, or trying to understand. From there Marquardt gets granular: open versus closed questions, how to sequence questions from broad to specific, how to use silence so the other person actually has room to think, and how active listening (paraphrasing, not interrupting, listening for what's not said) is inseparable from good questioning — a leader who asks well but doesn't listen well undoes the value of the question. The section closes with guidance on building a questioning culture deliberately: modeling it from the top, rewarding people who raise hard questions instead of punishing them, and building "questions for reflection" into routine meetings rather than treating questioning as a special event.

This hands off to Part III by noting that skill and culture only matter if they're applied to real leadership situations, which the book turns to next.
keyLessons: The Judger/Learner distinction matters more than question phrasing — the same question can build trust or trigger defensiveness depending on the asker's intent.
Silence after a question is a tool, not a gap to be filled by the leader.
A questioning culture has to be built deliberately through modeling and reward, not assumed to emerge on its own.

sections.title: A Guide for Leaders in Using Questions (Part III: application to supervision, coaching, problem-solving, and team-building)
sections.summary:
This closing part sets out to show questioning in action across the specific situations leaders actually face day to day: one-on-one supervision, coaching conversations, team-building, and structured problem-solving. Rather than staying abstract, Marquardt supplies concrete question sets for each context — for example, questions to open a coaching conversation without prescribing the answer, or questions to run a team through a stalled project without the leader taking over the diagnosis.

The substance draws heavily on the leader interviews woven throughout the book, showing how real executives at companies like DuPont, Alcoa, and Cargill used questions to onboard new hires, resolve conflict, and drive strategic planning sessions, with enough specificity that a reader can lift a question set and try it directly. A late chapter added in this edition focuses specifically on using questions for problem-solving, treating a facilitated question sequence as an alternative to a leader simply issuing a directive.

The book resolves by returning to its founding claim: leadership is not the possession of answers but the capacity to ask the question that unlocks the group's own answer, and organizations that build this capacity outperform those that rely on a single smart person at the top.
keyLessons: Different leadership situations (coaching, supervision, team-building, problem-solving) call for different question sets, not one generic approach.
A leader's job in a stalled discussion is often to keep asking rather than to jump in with the fix.
Real case examples from companies like DuPont and Cargill show questioning scales from individual conversations to organization-wide strategy work.
Default to asking before telling, especially when you already think you know the answer — you're often missing information your team has.
Diagnose your own mindset before you speak: are you entering this conversation as a Judger (evaluating, fixing) or a Learner (curious, open)?
Treat silence after a question as productive thinking time, not dead air to fill.
Build "questions for reflection" into routine meetings so questioning becomes habitual rather than exceptional.
Reward people who raise hard or uncomfortable questions instead of treating them as troublemakers.
Use open-ended questions to start a conversation and narrow to specifics only once the real issue has surfaced.
Pair every question with active listening — paraphrase back what you heard before responding or advising.
In a crisis or stalled project, resist prescribing the fix immediately; ask what the team sees before you decide.
Use structured question sequences (not just one good question) when coaching or running problem-solving sessions.
Model curiosity publicly as a leader — your team calibrates how safe questioning is by watching what you do, not what you say.

quotes.text: Leading with Questions examines why leaders often prefer to provide answers rather than ask questions and how limiting — and disastrous — that can be.
quotes.attribution: Michael J. Marquardt, Leading with Questions (publisher's chapter synopsis)

whoThisIsFor: Managers and executives who suspect their default communication style leans too heavily on directing rather than drawing out their team's own thinking.
whenToReadThis: Useful when stepping into a new leadership role, or when a team feels disengaged and the leader wants a concrete way to shift from telling to asking.

authorBio.name: Michael J. Marquardt
authorBio.bio:
Michael J. Marquardt is Professor Emeritus of Human and Organizational Learning at George Washington University, where he taught for decades in the fields of leadership, global management, and organizational learning. He built much of his academic and consulting reputation around "action learning," a problem-solving method that pairs real organizational challenges with structured group reflection and questioning, and he co-founded and served as first president of the World Institute of Action Learning.

Marquardt worked as a management consultant to a wide range of multinational corporations and government agencies, which gave him direct access to the executive interviews that anchor Leading with Questions. Across his career he wrote extensively — by his own account more than two dozen books — on leadership, global teams, and organizational learning, making him one of the more prolific academic voices in the action-learning field.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Judger vs. Learner Mindset
conceptsFrameworks.definition: A framework distinguishing two stances a person can bring into any conversation: the Judger mindset evaluates, blames, and looks to confirm existing conclusions, while the Learner mindset stays genuinely curious about what's true and possible. Marquardt argues the same question asked from these two mindsets produces opposite effects on trust and openness.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Questioning Culture
conceptsFrameworks.definition: An organizational environment, built deliberately by leaders through modeling and reward, in which asking questions — including hard or dissenting ones — is normalized rather than treated as a challenge to authority. Marquardt presents it as a measurable driver of engagement, innovation, and risk detection, not just a communication preference.
conceptsFrameworks.sourceSection: Part I, The Power of Questions

actionSteps: Before your next difficult conversation, write down one question you'd ask from a Judger stance and rewrite it from a Learner stance — notice the difference in tone before you speak.
In your next team meeting, replace one directive you'd normally give with a question and let the group sit in silence for at least five seconds before anyone (including you) fills it.
Add a single standing "questions for reflection" item to one recurring meeting this month and track whether it changes what surfaces.
Pick one recent decision you made unilaterally and identify who on your team you didn't ask — go ask them now, after the fact, what they would have said.
In your next coaching or feedback conversation, prepare three open questions in advance instead of a list of points to make.
reflectionQuestions: Where in your own leadership do you reach for an answer out of habit, even when you don't actually have better information than the people you're leading?
Think of a time a question from someone else changed your mind — what made you receptive to it rather than defensive?
Is there a topic in your organization right now that nobody feels safe enough to ask a hard question about? What would it take to change that?

points: Multiple reader reviews note the book is repetitive across chapters and could have made its case more succinctly — the argument for why questions matter is made at length before the practical "how" material arrives.

The evidence base leans heavily on leader self-report from interviews rather than controlled studies, so the causal claim that questioning cultures directly produce better business outcomes is plausible but not rigorously demonstrated.

Some of the framing (Judger vs. Learner) closely parallels other coaching literature (notably Marilee Adams's Change Your Questions, Change Your Life, whose author blurbed this book), so readers familiar with that tradition may find the core model less original than the book's presentation suggests.

The disaster case studies (Titanic, Challenger, Bay of Pigs) are used somewhat impressionistically to support the "lack of questioning" thesis; other historians attribute these failures to a wider mix of causes, and the book doesn't fully engage those alternative explanations.
criticalTake.contextNote: The book has gone through multiple editions (2005, 2014, and a 2023 third edition co-authored with Bob Tiede), with each edition adding new leader interviews and a chapter on problem-solving, suggesting the core framework has held up well enough to be extended rather than replaced.
